summary: Dipesh Chakrabarty promoted to a person entry, with contributions to postcolonial history (provincializing Europe, 1992–2000), Subaltern Studies (subaltern pasts and historical translation) and labour history (Bengal jute workers and Marx's categories, 1989, contested by Nair and Chandavarkar), a critique of Hobsbawm's 'prepolitical' as historicist (2000), and a post-2000 contribution to environmental history ('The Climate of History', 2009), marked post_2000. edge_742 no longer carries his name.
authorization: User, 2026-10-14: 'adding Chakrabarty is a very high priority'; and, the same day, 'we need to end the 2000 break in this project' (relayed by the coordinating session, which asked for the post-2000 environment edge).
rationale: Person entries go to thinkers whose frameworks students meet across fields (user, 2026-10-13). Provincializing Europe, the 'silent referent', the 'waiting room of history' and History 1 / History 2 are read across postcolonial, subaltern, labour and global history; he already holds roster rows in subaltern, post, labourhistory and social. In-period evidence: his 1989 preface and introduction, the 1992 Representations essay, the 1997 AHA essay, the 2000 introduction and Public Culture essay; criticism by Dirlik (1994), Chandavarkar (1997) and Sarkar (1997). The 2009 essay and its 2016 reception support only the post_2000 environment edge. Canadian-PhD uptake (52 of 1,303 strict History PhDs, 2009–2026) measures Canadian reading, not his importance (user).

edge_742.relationship: Subaltern Studies accounts of colonial workers' culture and consciousness taken into labour history, and contested there by labour historians (1989–97)
edge_742.map_label: Subaltern accounts of workers' culture, contested, 1989–97
edge_742.evidence_note: In-period evidence: Rajnarayan Chandavarkar, History Workshop Journal 43 (1997), pp. 177–196, read. 'While, at first, the subaltern historians borrowed liberally from Thompson's ideas, rhetoric and example, they seemed to take little account of wider developments in social history' (p. 182). 'The Subaltern followers of Thompson' espoused the view that rural migrants 'imported a peasant culture into the industrial setting' (p. 184), and 'some Subaltern historians mistook the received wisdom and commonplace of colonial officials for interpretative novelty' (p. 185); his note cites Arnold's 'Industrial Violence' as well as Chakrabarty (n. 32). Janaki Nair's 1990 review in International Labor and Working-Class History questions cultural determination and the treatment of gender (graph verification note; not re-read in 1.132). The arrow records one collective's labour histories and the criticism they drew in labour-history venues; it does not claim that labour history adopted the subaltern approach. Chakrabarty's own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.132).
